title: The Prophet
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Prophet sat in the market-place and told the fortunes of all who cared to engage his services. Suddenly there came running up one who told him that his house had been broken into by thieves, and that they had made off with everything they could lay hands on. He was up in a moment, and rushed off, tearing his hair and calling down curses on the miscreants. The bystanders were much amused, and one of them said, "Our friend professes to know what is going to happen to others, but it seems he's not clever enough to perceive what's in store for himself."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where did the Prophet sit to tell fortunes?
According to the passage, what news did the man bring the Prophet?
options: That his house had been broken into by thieves
That a fire had started nearby

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what had the thieves done?
options: Made off with everything they could lay hands on

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Prophet do upon hearing the news?
options: He rushed off, tearing his hair and calling down curses on the miscreants
He asked the bystanders for advice

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how did the bystanders react to the scene?
As the passage uses it, what does "miscreants" mean in "calling down curses on the miscreants"?
Based on the passage, why do the bystanders find the situation amusing?
options: They dislike the Prophet and enjoy his misfortune
The Prophet claims to foresee others' futures yet failed to foresee the theft of his own house
They think the Prophet is lying about the theft
They believe the thieves were actually his friends

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: Fortune-tellers should never work in public places
Someone who claims to know others' futures may be unable to foresee troubles in their own life
Thieves always target those who claim special knowledge
The market-place is a dangerous place to leave a house unattended

questions.prompt: According to the passage, whose fortunes did the Prophet tell?
options: All who cared to engage his services

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how did the man bring the news to the Prophet?
According to the passage, what exact words does the bystander use to describe the Prophet's failing?
options: "He is not clever enough to perceive what's in store for himself"
"He never learned the true art of prophecy"
"He is too old to practice his trade"
"He has angered the thieves on purpose"

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "professes" mean in "Our friend professes to know what is going to happen to others"?
Based on the passage, what contradiction does the bystander point out about the Prophet's trade?
options: He predicts events for strangers but failed to foresee misfortune in his own home
He charges too much money for his services
He tells fortunes only for people he dislikes
He refuses to tell his own fortune out of fear

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Prophet who tells others' fortunes learns his own house was robbed, prompting bystanders to mock his lack of self-knowledge
A Prophet correctly predicts a robbery before it happens
A Prophet is arrested for practicing fortune-telling in the market-place
Thieves rob the Prophet because he warned them of their own future
